The model’s value estimates were reset at the start of each task block, with the number of latent states at the start of each block being set to 1. The number of active latent states was used as an estimate of volatility, the log of the model’s expected value for the square of the prediction error was used as an estimate of noise. Model-derived trial labels (i.e. high/low volatility and noise) were calculated as for the analyses in Figure 4 of the main paper-- those trials with values above/below the mean value for that participant. Figure 3—figure supplement 1 illustrates the estimated learning rates of the latent-state model in the task blocks. As can be seen, it replicates the increased learning rate in high volatility blocks demonstrated by participants (F(1,696)=9.98, p=0.001), however, unlike participants, it significantly increases its learning rate in response to noise (F(1,696)=100, p<0.001). Using the labels for high/low volatility and noise derived from the latent-state model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) does not rescue normative behaviour in participants. Participants employ a higher learning rate in trials the model considers to have low relative to high volatility (F(1,556)=7, p=0.008), with no effect of noise (F(1,556)=3.1, p=0.08). These results suggest that, while the current latent-state model is able to capture some aspects of participant behaviour, the internal model estimates of unexpected and expected uncertainty (as markers of volatility and noise, respectively) do not explain the response to uncertainty accounted for by the Bayesian Observer Model. It should be noted that, while the latent state model was constructed to respond to levels of uncertainty (Cochran and Cisler, 2019) the formulation of these, and particularly of unexpected uncertainty is somewhat different to that used in the BOM (e.g. the estimate of unexpected uncertainty is a measure of the degree to which existing latent states are unable to account for experienced outcomes, and it can only increase across a block). It, therefore, remains possible that alternative latent state formulations would be more sensitive to the behaviour examined here. #### Performance of a simple RL model A final possibility considered is that some of the behaviour of the fitted BOM might be captured by a radically simpler model that does not represent levels of uncertainty. To assess this, we fitted the simple reinforcement learning model to all of a participant’s choices across all task blocks (i.e. as compared to the measurement RL model used in the main paper which was fit to individual blocks). We then estimated the effective learning rate per block using choices derived from this model and the same analysis pipeline as the main paper. As can be seen in Figure 2—figure supplement 3, this very simple model does not replicate the learning adaptation apparent in participant behaviour. ### Pupilometry data preprocessing Pupilometry data were collected using the Eyelink II system (SRresearch) from both eyes, sampled at 500 Hz. Preprocessing involved the following steps: Eye blinks were identified using the built-in filter of the Eyelink system and were removed from the data. A linear interpolation was implemented for all missing data points (including blinks). The resulting trace was subjected to a low pass Butterworth filter (cut-off of 3.75 Hz), z-transformed across the session (Browning et al., 2015; Nassar et al., 2012), and then averaged across the two eyes. The pupil response to the win and the loss outcomes were extracted separately from each trial, using a time window based on the presentation of the outcomes. This included a 2 s pre-outcome period, and a 6 s period following outcome presentation. Individual trials were excluded from the pupilometry analysis if more than 50% of the data from the outcome period had been interpolated (mean = 6.7% of trials) (Browning et al., 2015). The first five trials from each block were not used in the analysis as initial pupil adaptation can occur in response to luminance changes in this period (Browning et al., 2015; Nassar et al., 2012). The preprocessing resulted in two sets of timeseries per participant, one set containing pupil size data for each included trial when the win outcomes were displayed and the other when the loss outcomes were displayed. These pupil area data were binned into 1 s bins across the outcome period for analysis (NB Figure 5a–f). This analysis was supplemented by an individual regression approach (Figure 5g–i) in which individual participants’ pupil area timeseries was first regressed against estimated trialwise volatility and noise from the intact BOM (Figure 5g), as well as a number of control variables (constant term, amount won/lost on trial (i.e. magnitude of outcome), valence of outcome (win or loss), order in which outcomes were presented (win first/loss first), trial number (1:360), whether shape chosen switched on next trial or not (1:0)). The residuals from this regression were then regressed against estimated trial-wise volatility and noise from the degraded BOM (Figure 5h and i). These regression analyses resulted in timeseries of beta-weights that were analysed in the same manner as raw pupil size data. ### Quantification and statistical analysis Behavioural data were analysed using linear mixed effect models (fitlme function of Matlab (2022a)) with participant ID included as a random factor and volatility, noise, and valence added as fixed factors. Two-way interactions between fixed effects were also tested (main effects are reported from models without interaction terms). Addition of random slopes for any of the fixed factors decreased LME model fit statistics and so were not included (Matuschek et al., 2017). Analysis of timeseries pupillometry data included the additional fixed effect factor of time across the outcome period. Learning rates were transformed to the infinite real line using a logistic transform before analyses (untransformed data are displayed in figures for ease of interpretation). The normality of the distribution of the residuals of the LME analyses was checked both visually and with a one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Changes in the classification of trials between the full and degraded BOM (Figure 4b) were analysed using a repeated measures ANOVA with within-subject factors of volatility, noise, and valence. Raw data are superimposed on all summary figures.

The authors present an interesting study using RL and Bayesian modelling to examine differences in learning rate adaptation in conditions of high and low volatility and noise respectively. The experimental task used is cleverly designed and does a good job of manipulating both volatility and noise. ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.103734.3.sa2](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.103734.3.sa2)

Summary:

In this study, the authors aimed to investigate how humans learn and adapt their behavior in dynamic environments characterized by two distinct types of uncertainty: volatility (systematic changes in outcomes) and noise (random variability in outcomes). Specifically, they sought to understand how participants adjust their learning rates in response to changes in these forms of uncertainty.

To achieve this, the authors employed a two-step approach:

Reinforcement Learning (RL) Model:

They first used an RL model to fit participants' behavior, revealing that the learning rate was context-dependent-it varied based on the levels of volatility and noise. However, the RL model showed that participants misattributed noise as volatility, leading to higher learning rates in noisy conditions, where the optimal strategy would be to be less sensitive to random fluctuations.

Bayesian Observer Model (BOM):

To better account for this context dependency, they introduced a Bayesian Observer Model (BOM), which models how an ideal Bayesian learner would update their beliefs about environmental uncertainty. They found that a degraded version of the BOM, where the agent had a coarser representation of noise compared to volatility, best fit the participants' behavior. This suggested that participants were not fully distinguishing between noise and volatility, instead treating noise as volatility and adjusting their learning rates accordingly.

The authors also aimed to use pupillometry data (measuring pupil dilation) as a physiological marker to arbitrate between models and understand how participants' internal representations of uncertainty influenced both their behavior and physiological responses. Their objective was to explore whether the BOM could explain not just behavioral choices but also these physiological responses, thereby providing stronger evidence for the model's validity.

Overall, the study sought to reconcile approximate rationality in human learning by showing that participants still follow a Bayesian-like learning process, but with simplified internal models that lead to suboptimal decisions in noisy environments.

Strengths:

The generative model presented in the study is both innovative and insightful. The authors first employ a Reinforcement Learning (RL) model to fit participants' behavior, revealing that the learning rate is context-dependent-specifically, it varies based on the levels of volatility and noise in the task. They then introduce a Bayesian Observer Model (BOM) to account for this context dependency, ultimately finding that a degraded BOM-in which the agent has a coarser representation of noise compared to volatility-provides the best fit to the participants' behavior. This suggests that participants are not fully distinguishing between noise and volatility, leading to misattribution of noise as volatility. Consequently, participants adopt higher learning rates even in noisy contexts, where an optimal strategy would involve being less sensitive to new information (i.e., using lower learning rates). This finding highlights a rational but approximate learning process, as described in the paper.

Weaknesses:

While the RL and Bayesian models both successfully predict behavior, it remains unclear how to fully reconcile the two approaches. The RL model captures behavior in terms of a fixed or context-dependent learning rate, while the BOM provides a more nuanced account with dynamic updates based on volatility and noise. Both models can predict actions when fit appropriately, but the pupillometry data offers a promising avenue to arbitrate between the models. However, the current study does not provide a direct comparison between the RL framework and the Bayesian model in terms of how well they explain the pupillometry data. It would be valuable to see whether the RL model can also account for physiological markers of learning, such as pupil responses, or if the BOM offers a unique advantage in this regard. A comparison of the two models using pupillometry data could strengthen the argument for the BOM's superiority, as currently, the possibility that RL models could explain the physiological data remains unexplored.

The model comparison between the Bayesian Observer Model and the self-defined degraded internal model could be further enhanced. Since different assumptions about the internal model's structure lead to varying levels of model complexity, using a formal criterion such as Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) or Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) would allow for a more rigorous comparison of model fit. Including such comparisons would ensure that the degraded BOM is not simply favored due to its flexibility or higher complexity, but rather because it genuinely captures the participants' behavioral and physiological data better than alternative models. This would also help address concerns about overfitting and provide a clearer justification for using the degraded BOM over other potential models.

results.result: 70 participants completed a learning task with independently manipulated volatility and noise across six blocks of 60 trials each. Participants successfully learned the task, selecting the most rewarded option on 71% of trials. The study was adequately powered (d=0.35, 80% power) and received ethical approval.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C62 provide comprehensive methodological details including sample size, task structure, ethical approval, and participant performance. The power analysis (C45-C46) justifies the sample size, and the task design (C41-C57) is clearly described with appropriate controls and manipulations.

results.result: Participants adapted their learning rates normatively to volatility (higher learning rates when volatility was high, F(1,696)=22.2, p<0.001) but showed no main effect of noise (F(1,696)=0.63, p=0.43). A significant volatility×noise interaction (F(1,693)=7.74, p=0.006) revealed that noise increased learning rates when volatility was low but not when volatility was high.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C11 report consistent statistical findings with appropriate F-statistics and p-values. The pattern shows expected adaptation to volatility but unexpected responses to noise, with the interaction effect properly characterized through follow-up analyses (C10-C11).

results.result: The intact Bayesian Observer Model (BOM) adapted normatively to both volatility and noise. Lesioning the BOM by removing volatility or noise adaptation did not replicate participant behavior. However, degrading the BOM's representation of uncertainty—with greater coarsening of noise than volatility (F(1,69)=49, p<0.001)—better matched participant learning rates and was favored by BIC scores.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 describe a systematic model comparison approach with appropriate statistical support. The degraded BOM provides a mechanistic explanation for participant behavior through differential precision in representing noise versus volatility, supported by model comparison metrics (C15) and miscategorization analyses (C16-C18).

results.result: When trials were labeled using the degraded BOM's estimates rather than task block structure, participants showed normative learning rate adaptation—increasing learning rates when the degraded model estimated high volatility (F(1,566)=86, p<0.001) and low noise (F(1,566)=81, p<0.001). This pattern was not observed with intact BOM labels, suggesting participants adapt to imprecise estimates of noise that lead to its misattribution as volatility.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20, C28, and C80 demonstrate that the degraded BOM captures participant behavior through trial relabeling. The control analysis (C20) strengthens the interpretation by showing this effect is specific to the degraded model. This provides strong evidence for the main conclusion about imprecise noise estimation.

results.result: Pupil size did not vary normatively with task block structure (no effect of volatility: F(1,1723)=0.002, p=0.9; opposite effect of noise: F(1,1723)=13.8, p<0.001). However, when trials were labeled by the degraded BOM's estimates, pupil size increased normatively with high volatility (F(1,2067)=105, p<0.001) and low noise (F(1,2067)=42.3, p<0.001). The degraded model explained additional variance in pupil data beyond the intact model for noise (F(1,286)=4.1, p=0.04) but not volatility.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 and C91 provide converging physiological evidence supporting the degraded BOM. The hierarchical regression analysis (C23) demonstrates that the degraded model captures variance in pupil responses not explained by the intact model, specifically for noise estimation, validating the behavioral findings.

results.result: The best-fitting reinforcement learning measurement model included separate learning rates for win and loss outcomes. Inverse temperature decreased with higher noise but was not affected by volatility. Including inverse temperature as a covariate did not alter the main learning rate findings. Appropriate statistical checks (normality tests, logistic transformation) were performed.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65, C77-C78 describe appropriate model selection and statistical procedures. The control analysis (C65) demonstrates robustness of the main findings to potential confounds from choice stochasticity.

results.result: The BOM was provided with all trial outcomes (excluding practice block), treated win and loss outcomes independently, and reset beliefs about outcome magnitudes at the start of each block while maintaining beliefs about volatility and noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 describe appropriate implementation details for the BOM that account for the task structure (changing stimuli between blocks). These methodological choices are justified by the task design.

results.result: An alternative latent-state model captured the volatility effect in participant behavior (F(1,696)=9.98, p=0.001) but, unlike participants, increased learning rates with noise (F(1,696)=100, p<0.001). Using latent-state model trial labels did not rescue normative behavior in participants.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 demonstrate that an alternative computational approach does not explain participant behavior as well as the degraded BOM. This strengthens the main findings by ruling out a competing explanation, though the authors appropriately note that other latent-state formulations might perform better.

results.result: Pupillometry data underwent standard preprocessing including blink removal, linear interpolation, low-pass filtering, and z-scoring. Trials with >50% interpolated data were excluded (mean 6.7%), and the first five trials of each block were excluded to avoid luminance adaptation effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 describe standard and appropriate preprocessing procedures for pupillometry data, with citations supporting the rationale for specific choices (C76). The exclusion criteria are reasonable and clearly stated.

results.result: Efficient learning requires adapting to different forms of uncertainty. Normatively, learning rates should increase when volatility is high (to track changes) and when noise is low (to weight reliable information more heavily).
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27, C29, and C44 state well-established normative principles from learning theory, supported by appropriate citations (C29). These provide the theoretical foundation for the experimental predictions.

results.result: Previous studies consistently found increased learning rates with higher volatility. However, normative responses to noise have only been observed when noise was explicitly signaled or unambiguously different from volatility. Prior work by the authors showed appropriate volatility adaptation regardless of outcome valence.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C30-C31 accurately characterize the prior literature with appropriate citations. This establishes the novelty of the current study in examining noise adaptation when volatility and noise are not easily discriminable.

results.result: Theoretical frameworks propose that noradrenergic/locus coeruleus activity signals volatility while cholinergic activity represents noise. Pupil dilation correlates with LC activity in primates and has been associated with volatility in humans, though it also responds to other signals like surprise. The pupillary signal may reflect general belief updating rather than specific volatility, predicting that pupil size should increase with both high volatility and low noise.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 provide appropriate theoretical background with citations supporting each point. The inference about pupil size reflecting general belief updating (C37) is reasonable given the cited evidence, leading to a testable prediction (C38).

results.result: The task was designed so that high volatility/low noise and low volatility/high noise conditions produced similar ranges of outcome magnitudes, requiring participants to discriminate uncertainty sources based on temporal structure rather than magnitude ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C43 and C57 describe a key design feature that distinguishes this study from prior work. Figure 1b provides visual confirmation of similar magnitude ranges across conditions, supporting this claim.

results.result: Human learners are relatively insensitive to changes in outcome noise, making internally consistent errors by misattributing noise as volatility. This leads to suboptimal choice and occurs when volatility and noise are not unambiguously different.
results.evaluation: Claims C79, C81-C82, and C85 represent the main conclusions of the study, well-supported by the behavioral findings (C6-C11), modeling results (C12-C20), and pupillometry data (C21-C23). The inference about suboptimal choice (C82) follows logically from the misattribution.

results.result: The absence of normative noise adaptation contrasts with previous studies where noise was explicitly signaled or unambiguous. A recent study in visual perception also found insensitivity to noise, suggesting this may be a general feature of human decision-making rather than specific to learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to prior work. However, the generalization to all decision-making (C87) is speculative, based on a single study in a different domain (C86). More evidence would be needed to support this broader claim.

results.result: Noise fundamentally limits information reliability, and ignoring it has detrimental effects on inference. Evidence shows humans can respond normatively to noise when it is unambiguous, making complete insensitivity unlikely.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 provide appropriate theoretical context with citations. The argument that complete insensitivity would be surprising given the importance of noise and evidence for normative responses under some conditions is logically sound.

results.result: The pupillometry signal reflects general belief updating rather than specifically volatility, as it responds to both volatility and noise. Distinct behavioral and physiological responses to the two forms of uncertainty suggest separable neural representations are maintained.
results.evaluation: Claims C92 and C100 draw reasonable inferences from the pupillometry findings (C21-C23) and are supported by citations to prior work (C92). The inference about separable neural representations (C100) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging the study cannot directly address neural implementation.

results.result: The BOM provides an algorithmic description of how the task may be solved but likely does not describe cognitive or neural implementation. Alternative approaches exist, including simpler methods that may be more plausible. The results indicate relative insensitivity to noise but do not specify underlying mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C96 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the modeling approach. The authors correctly distinguish between algorithmic-level descriptions and implementation-level mechanisms, noting that alternative formulations exist (C95) and that the study identifies the phenomenon but not the mechanism (C96).

results.result: Previous neuroimaging work has examined one form of uncertainty at a time. An analogy to neuronal decoding suggests that signal-correlation (tracking volatility) and noise-correlation (independent covariation) may provide a framework for understanding how different uncertainty types are encoded.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C99 provide appropriate context about prior neuroimaging work (C97) and offer a speculative but reasonable analogy to neuronal decoding literature (C98-C99). This is presented as a possibility rather than a conclusion, which is appropriate given the study's focus on behavior.

results.result: The reinforcement learning measurement model fitted separately to blocks does not account for learning adaptation across blocks, as it measures rather than models the adaptation process.
results.evaluation: Claim C101 appropriately clarifies the purpose and limitations of the measurement model. This distinction between measurement and mechanistic models is important for interpreting the results and is correctly stated.

results.result: The study employed a cleverly designed learning task with 70 participants in which volatility and noise were independently manipulated across blocks. The task required participants to distinguish whether outcome variability was caused by volatility or noise based on temporal structure rather than magnitude of changes, with similar ranges of outcome magnitudes for high noise and high volatility conditions.
results.evaluation: All reviewers praised the experimental design. The editor noted it was 'cleverly designed' and one reviewer stated 'The experimental task used is cleverly designed and does a good job of manipulating both volatility and noise.' No concerns were raised about the task design, sample size, or methodological approach.

results.result: Participants showed a significant main effect of volatility on learning rates (higher learning rates when volatility was high), but no main effect of noise. There was a significant interaction between volatility and noise, with an unexpected effect of noise in the opposite direction (outcomes influencing choice more when noise increased).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these behavioral findings without challenge. One reviewer summarized: 'the RL model showed that participants misattributed noise as volatility, leading to higher learning rates in noisy conditions.' The editor noted the study demonstrates 'humans adapt learning rates rationally to environmental volatility yet systematically misattribute noise as volatility.'

results.result: The intact Bayesian Observer Model (BOM) adapted normatively to both volatility and noise, but lesioned versions did not recapitulate participant behavior. A degraded BOM with coarser representation of noise than volatility better matched participant learning rates, showing greater coarsening of the noise dimension and causing the model to miscategorize high noise trials as high volatility.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the modeling approach. One reviewer stated 'The modelling approach takes an interesting and creative approach to understand the source of apparently suboptimal adaptation of learning rates to noise, through carefully "lesioning" an optimal Bayesian model.' The editor highlighted 'innovative lesion-based comparisons between reinforcement-learning and degraded Bayesian Observer Models' as a strength.

results.result: When trial labels from the degraded BOM were used, participants showed normative responses to uncertainty (increasing learning rates when estimated volatility was high and noise was low). This pattern was not observed with intact BOM labels, demonstrating that participants adapt to estimated noise but with imprecise estimates that lead to misattribution as volatility.
results.evaluation: This core finding was accepted by all reviewers. One reviewer noted the study 'reveal[s] that apparently suboptimal adaptation of learning rates results from incorrectly detecting volatility in the environment when it is not in fact present.' The editor emphasized this demonstrates 'approximate rationality with simplified internal models.'

results.result: Pupillometry data showed that participants' pupils did not adapt normatively to task block structure, but when analyzed using degraded BOM trial labels, the expected increases in pupil size in response to both raised volatility and reduced noise were recovered. The degraded model accounted for variance in pupil responses to noise not explained by the intact model.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the pupillometry findings as convergent evidence. The editor noted 'convergent behavioural and pupillometric data' as a strength. One reviewer initially requested 'a direct comparison between the RL framework and the Bayesian model in terms of how well they explain the pupillometry data,' but later confirmed 'The authors have addressed all my questions.'

results.result: The study employed multiple modeling approaches including reinforcement learning models fitted to separate blocks, an intact Bayesian Observer Model, and a latent-state model. The RL model included separate learning rates for win and loss outcomes, and various preprocessing and analysis procedures were applied to both behavioral and pupillometry data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the methodological details without substantive critique. One reviewer noted 'The model space could be more extensive, although the authors have covered the most relevant models for the question at hand,' indicating acceptance of the modeling choices. Another reviewer initially requested 'formal model comparisons (e.g., BIC/AIC)' but later confirmed all questions were addressed.

results.result: The study concludes that human learners are relatively insensitive to changes in outcome noise and make internally consistent errors by misattributing environmental noise as volatility, leading to suboptimal choices. This insensitivity occurs when noise and volatility are not unambiguously different, though the study does not specify the lower-level mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these conclusions. The editor stated the study 'makes an important contribution by showing that humans adapt learning rates rationally to environmental volatility yet systematically misattribute noise as volatility, demonstrating approximate rationality with simplified internal models.' One reviewer noted the findings 'highlight a rational but approximate learning process.'

results.result: The study is grounded in normative predictions from learning theory: efficient learning requires adaptation to different forms of uncertainty, with learning rates increasing when volatility is high and/or noise is low, and decreasing when noise is high.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these theoretical foundations without question. The normative framework was treated as established knowledge that provided the basis for evaluating participant behavior.

results.result: The manuscript situates findings within existing literature on learning under uncertainty, noting that while many studies have found increased learning rates in response to volatility, normative responses to noise have only been observed when noise is explicitly signaled or unambiguous. The study also discusses theoretical frameworks linking neurotransmitter systems to uncertainty estimation and pupillary responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the characterization of prior literature or theoretical frameworks. The literature review was implicitly accepted as providing appropriate context for the current findings.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that the BOM is an algorithmic description of how the task may be solved rather than a description of cognitive or neural implementation, and note that alternative algorithmic approaches exist. They suggest that distinct behavioral and physiological responses to volatility and noise indicate separable neural representations are maintained.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these limitations and interpretations. The acknowledgment of the BOM as an algorithmic rather than implementational model was not challenged, and the inference about separable neural representations was consistent with reviewers' acceptance of the distinct behavioral and physiological findings.

Complete alignment on modeling approach (C12-C18). Both evaluations praise the degraded BOM and systematic model comparison. Peer reviewers specifically highlight the 'creative approach' of lesioning the optimal model, matching OpenEval's positive assessment.

Full concordance on core finding about trial relabeling and misattribution (C19-C20, C28, C80). Both evaluations support this as the central result demonstrating imprecise noise estimation. Peer reviewers emphasize 'approximate rationality with simplified internal models.'

Strong agreement on pupillometry findings (C21-C23, C91). Both evaluations accept these as convergent physiological evidence.
